1079.title: The iqamah
1079.hook: the second call, just before prayer begins
1079.howItsDone: In the mosque, someone calls the iqamah just before the congregational prayer starts; the worshipers stand, form straight rows behind the imam, and the prayer begins. It may also be said by someone about to pray alone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adhan's words, and a line: come to success. The adhan says the time has come. Today, the call that says now.

Inside a mosque, a few minutes after the adhan. The room is loose and quiet. A teenager scrolls his phone by the wall. Two old friends murmur near the back. Someone prays a couple of units alone in a corner. A boy ties and reties his shoelace for no reason. Then a man near the front stands and starts a second call, quicker than the first, flatter, almost brisk. And the whole room changes shape. Phones go into pockets. People rise, step forward, line up shoulder to shoulder, and close the gaps between them. By the time he finishes, there are rows where there was a crowd.
screen: `A LOOSE, QUIET ROOM.` → `A SECOND CALL, QUICKER.` → `ROWS WHERE THERE WAS A CROWD.`

segments.voice: That second call is the iqamah. The adhan goes out to the street: the time has come, wherever you are, come. The iqamah is for the room: the prayer is starting, here, now. Its words mostly follow the adhan, and Sahih al-Bukhari, number 605, records how Bilal was told to say them: the adhan's phrases in pairs, the iqamah's singly, except for one new line that the adhan doesn't have. Qad qamati as-salah. The prayer has stood up. It has begun. The Hanafi school says the iqamah's phrases in pairs, like the adhan, and the other Sunni schools say most of them singly; each follows reports it trusts. Between the two calls there's a space. In Sahih al-Bukhari, number 624, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that between every two calls there is a prayer, for whoever wants it: a waiting room with a door already open. And how should you arrive when you hear the iqamah? A sprint might seem right. The hadith says the opposite. Sahih al-Bukhari, number 636: when you hear the iqamah, walk to the prayer with calm and dignity, don't hurry; whatever you catch, pray it, and whatever you missed, complete it afterward. So the call that says now doesn't mean panic. It means stand, step in, and join the row as you are. The adhan gathers people from far away. The iqamah gathers the people already in the room into one line.
screen: `THE ADHAN FOR THE STREET, THE IQAMAH FOR THE ROOM.` · `QAD QAMATI AS-SALAH: IT HAS BEGUN.` · `BETWEEN THE TWO CALLS, A PRAYER.` · `WALK, DON'T RUN.` · then, large: `THE PRAYER HAS STOOD UP.`

segments.voice: If you're sitting, notice the looseness of waiting first; then, without rushing, stand and feel your feet take your weight, your shoulders settle, your hands rest. Stay standing, or sit again if you need to, and breathe slowly in the space after the call. If you pray, you can stand this way at your next prayer, calm, not hurried; if not, this is simply the difference between waiting and beginning.
Iqamah. The second call, said in the room just before the prayer begins, with its own line: the prayer has stood up. Today's word.
Your line: stand now. Calm, not a sprint. I'll be here tomorrow.

1080.title: The sunnah prayers
1080.hook: regular extra units before and after the obligatory ones
1080.howItsDone: Muslims who keep the rawatib pray short voluntary units before or after the obligatory prayers, at home or in the mosque, following the pattern their school teaches, and give particular care to the two units before the dawn prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the iqamah: stand now, calm, not a sprint. Before it, there was a space for a prayer. Today, what fills it.

Better than the world and everything in it. That's a big claim to make about two short units of prayer, said quietly in a dark bedroom before the dawn prayer, with the alarm still blinking and nobody watching. Aishah reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying exactly that about the two units before the dawn prayer, in Sahih Muslim, number 725. Not the obligatory prayer. The small extra one before it. Today, the prayers that sit around the obligatory ones like a frame around a picture.
screen: `BETTER THAN THE WORLD.` → `TWO SHORT UNITS, BEFORE DAWN.` → `A FRAME AROUND A PICTURE.`

segments.voice: The word is rawatib, the regular ones: the voluntary prayers the Prophet ﷺ kept attached to the obligatory prayers, some just before, some just after. Not required, but not random either. In Sahih Muslim, number 728, his wife Umm Habibah reports him saying that whoever prays twelve units a day and night, beyond the obligatory, will have a house built for them in the garden. And Umm Habibah adds that she never stopped praying them after she heard it. Jami at-Tirmidhi, number 415, lays out where those units fall: four before the noon prayer and two after it, two after the sunset prayer, two after the night prayer, and two before dawn. Another companion, Ibn Umar, in Sahih al-Bukhari, number 1180, remembers ten, with two before noon instead of four. The schools follow these reports in slightly different ways, and Shia practice keeps its own pattern of daily voluntary prayers. Among all of them, one pair gets special weight. Aishah says, in Sahih al-Bukhari, number 1169, that the Prophet ﷺ was not more careful about any voluntary prayer than the two before dawn. Why pray what isn't required? One answer is in the word sunnah itself: following how he actually prayed, not only what was demanded. Another is in a hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud, number 864: on the day of reckoning, if the obligatory prayers fall short, the voluntary ones are looked to, to make up what's missing. The frame protects the picture.
screen: `RAWATIB: THE REGULAR ONES.` · `UMM HABIBAH: TWELVE, A HOUSE IN THE GARDEN.` · `THE TWO BEFORE DAWN, KEPT MOST CAREFULLY.` · `THE FRAME PROTECTS THE PICTURE.` · then, large: `BETTER THAN THE WORLD AND ALL IN IT.`

segments.voice: Picture tomorrow morning: the alarm, the dark, the minute before the dawn prayer or before your day begins, and see yourself adding something small and extra there, before the main thing. If you pray, those are the two units before fajr, and you can settle now on praying them; if you don't, choose a two-minute habit to set before the first big task of your day. Then sit quietly with the decision made.
Rawatib. The regular voluntary prayers, before and after the obligatory ones, with the two before dawn kept most carefully of all. Today's word.
Your line: the sunnah around it. Small, extra, and kept, the way Umm Habibah kept hers. Up next: the odd prayer.

1081.title: The odd prayer
1081.hook: the odd-numbered night prayer, strongly stressed, wajib in the Hanafi school
1081.howItsDone: Muslims pray witr after the night prayer and before dawn, as one, three or more units so the total is odd; some pray it before sleep and some at the end of the night, and the Hanafi school counts it as wajib while the other Sunni schools treat it as a strongly stressed sunnah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rawatib, the sunnah around the obligatory prayers, with the two before dawn kept most carefully. Today, the prayer that closes the night.

Abu Hurayrah once said his close friend had advised him to keep three things until he died. His close friend was the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The three: fasting three days every month, praying two units in the late morning, and praying witr before going to sleep. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the list, at number 1178. Two of those are about daylight. The last is about the moment just before you turn out the light, the phone on the charger, the day nearly done.
screen: `ADVICE TO KEEP UNTIL DEATH.` → `FAST, PRAY IN THE MORNING, PRAY WITR.` → `A PRAYER AT THE EDGE OF SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Witr means odd, as in an odd number. It's the prayer with an odd count of units that closes the night's praying: one, or three, or more, so long as the total comes out odd. Why odd? In Sahih al-Bukhari, number 6410, the Prophet ﷺ says that Allah is witr, and loves witr. The same word that names this prayer is used of God: single, one, not paired. Some teachers read ending the night on an odd number as a small sign of that oneness, the tawhid this path has already met, written into the shape of a prayer. When is it prayed? Any time after the night prayer, isha, until dawn. In Sahih al-Bukhari, number 998, he says: make witr the last of your prayer at night. And Sahih Muslim, number 755, gives a practical choice. Whoever fears they won't wake in the last part of the night should pray witr before sleeping. Whoever expects to wake can pray it at the end, because prayer at the end of the night is witnessed. That's Abu Hurayrah's choice in the hook: witr before sleep, so it's never lost. How binding is it? Here the schools differ, and they say so openly. The Hanafi school holds witr to be wajib, necessary, a step below the obligatory prayers but not to be dropped. The other Sunni schools hold it to be a strongly stressed sunnah, not obligatory. Either way, it's the prayer the day ends on.
screen: `WITR: AN ODD NUMBER OF UNITS.` · `ALLAH IS WITR AND LOVES WITR.` · `LAST OF THE NIGHT, OR BEFORE SLEEP.` · `WAJIB FOR HANAFIS, STRONGLY STRESSED FOR OTHERS.` · then, large: `MAKE WITR THE LAST OF YOUR PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Let the day slow down. If you pray, you can settle now on praying witr tonight before sleep, even a single unit, so the night ends on it; if you don't, count your breaths slowly, one, two, three, and stop on an odd number. One last breath, alone and unpaired, then rest in what's left of the quiet.
Witr. Odd. The prayer with an odd number of units that ends the night, wajib for the Hanafi school and strongly stressed for the other Sunni schools. Today's word.
Your line: end the night odd. One breath, unpaired, and the day is done. Go gently.

1082.title: The night prayer
1082.hook: prayer after sleeping and waking in the night
1082.howItsDone: Muslims who keep tahajjud usually sleep first, then rise in the later part of the night, make wudu and pray voluntary units in pairs, often finishing with witr before the dawn prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, witr: the odd prayer that closes the night. Today we stay in the night.

A quarter past three in the morning. The house is dark, the phone face-down, the fridge humming to itself. Someone gets out of a warm bed, not because a baby cried or a dream went wrong. On purpose. Cold water on the hands and face for wudu. A mat unrolled in the corner of the bedroom. No adhan calls this prayer. Nobody at the mosque will notice who came. The street is asleep, and that's part of the point. It's a prayer you go to sleep before, and then get up for.
screen: `A QUARTER PAST THREE.` → `UP ON PURPOSE.` → `NO ADHAN CALLS THIS ONE.`

segments.voice: Tahajjud is the voluntary prayer of the night, prayed after you've slept and woken. First, the Qur'an, where it begins as words to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself. Pickthall's translation of surah seventeen: "And some part of the night awake for it, a largess for thee." A largess: a gift beyond what was owed. The five daily prayers are the duty; this one is the gift on top. Second, the people the Qur'an describes, in surah thirty-two: those "Who forsake their beds to cry unto their Lord in fear and hope." It's an honest picture. The bed is warm, and leaving it costs something. Third, why the dark hours. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says that every night, when its last third remains, God asks: who is calling on Me, so that I may answer? Who is asking, so that I may give? Who seeks forgiveness, so that I may forgive? Some readers hear the timing as an invitation: the quietest hour is the one the hadith describes as open. Fourth, one life. Aisha, his wife, saw the Prophet stand in the night prayer until his feet swelled, and asked why, when he had already been forgiven. He answered with a question: should I not be a grateful servant? The night prayer isn't a debt paid down. It's thanks. And since the hadith asks that witr be the last of the night's prayer, tahajjud comes first, and the night still closes odd. Some keep it often, some in hard seasons, some in Ramadan, some rarely. The gift is described the same way for all of them.

segments.voice: Picture one night this week when you might wake: the dark room, the cold water, the corner where you'd stand. If you pray, set your intention now to rise after sleeping and pray two units. If you don't, you might set an alarm a few minutes early and spend them awake and quiet, before the day gets a say.
Tahajjud. The voluntary night prayer, prayed after sleeping and waking, a gift beyond the duty. Today's word.

1083.title: The forenoon prayer
1083.hook: a voluntary prayer when the sun is up
1083.howItsDone: Muslims who keep the duha prayer pray at least two voluntary units after the sun has risen well and before the time of the noon prayer, often at work, at home, or in the mosque after a morning class.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tahajjud: the night prayer, a gift on top of the duty. Now the sun comes up.

"By the morning hours." That's how Pickthall opens surah ninety-three, and the Arabic word behind those morning hours is today's word. Duha is not dawn. Dawn has its prayer, fajr, prayed in the gray before sunrise. Duha comes later: the sun fully up, the commute done, the first coffee gone, the inbox filling. The middle of the morning, the stretch easiest to stop noticing. Islam puts a prayer there too, and nobody is required to pray it.
screen: `BY THE MORNING HOURS.` → `NOT DAWN: LATER.` → `NOBODY IS REQUIRED TO PRAY IT.`

segments.voice: Duha is a voluntary prayer, prayed after the sun has risen well into the sky and before the heat of noon. Its smallest form is two units. First, the hour has a surah. Surah ninety-three swears by the morning hours and the stillness of the night, then tells the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that his Lord has not left him. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari ties it to a time when he had fallen ill and missed his night prayers, and someone taunted him that he'd been abandoned. So the forenoon, in that surah, is a sign of being remembered. Second, a hadith in Sahih Muslim gives the prayer a surprising job. Every morning, it says, a charity is owed for each joint of your body. Every glorifying of God is a charity, every word of praise, every good deed urged and every wrong discouraged. And two units prayed in the forenoon are enough for all of it. Your knuckles, your knees, your jaw: two units cover the thanks. Third, a witness. Umm Hani reported that on the day Mecca was opened, he bathed in her house and prayed eight units in the forenoon, lighter than any prayer she'd seen from him, yet with full bowing and prostration. Fourth, the timing has a picture. Another report in Sahih Muslim calls it the prayer of those who often turn back to God, and says its time is when the young camels feel the heat of the sand. Scholars give the window in hours and minutes now; the hadith gives it in hot sand.
screen: `THE HOUR HAS A SURAH.` · `A CHARITY FOR EVERY JOINT.` · `UMM HANI SAW EIGHT.` · `WHEN YOUNG CAMELS FEEL THE HEAT.`

segments.voice: Slowly open and close your hands, roll your shoulders, flex your feet: each joint is one of the charities the hadith counts. If you pray, you can plan two units of duha for later this morning, or pray them now if the sun is up. If you don't, let each joint you move be one thank-you, said without words.
Duha. The forenoon, when the sun is well up, and the voluntary prayer prayed in it. Today's word.
Your line: the forenoon prayer. Two units, and every joint is thanked. That's today, done.

1084.title: The prayer of seeking guidance
1084.hook: two units and a du'a when deciding (Bukhari)
1084.howItsDone: Muslims facing a decision pray two voluntary units and then recite the istikharah du'a taught in Sahih al-Bukhari, naming the matter in it; then they go ahead, often after asking advice from people they trust.

segments.voice: Yesterday, duha: two units in the busy middle of the morning. Today, a prayer for when you can't decide.

Two job offers sit in two browser tabs. Or it's a lease, a move back home, a person a family has suggested, or whether to say yes to a surgery. A list of pros and cons has been written twice and torn up once. A companion named Jabir said the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ taught them a prayer for exactly this, in all their affairs, the way he taught them a surah of the Qur'an. Not only the huge decisions. All of them.
screen: `TWO OFFERS, TWO TABS.` → `THE LIST TORN UP ONCE.` → `TAUGHT LIKE A SURAH.`

segments.voice: Istikharah means asking God to choose the good. First, the form, from the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari: when one of you is concerned about a matter, pray two units that are not the obligatory prayer, then make this du'a. Second, the words, described rather than recited here. The person asks God to choose for them by His knowledge and give them ability by His power, because God has power and they have none, God knows and they do not. Then the heart of it: if this matter, named here, is good for me in my religion, my living and how my affairs turn out, decree it for me and make it easy. If it is bad for me, turn it away from me, and turn me away from it. Then decree the good for me wherever it is, and make me content with it. It doesn't only ask for the right door. It asks to be at peace with whichever door opens. Third, what the hadith doesn't say. It mentions no dream, no sign in the sky, no rush of certainty. Scholars describe the answer in different ways. Some say go ahead with what you were leaning toward and watch whether the way is made easy or blocked. Some speak of the heart settling. Some advise pairing it with asking people you trust. Fourth, why hand a choice over. Pickthall's translation of surah two: "it may happen that ye hate a thing which is good for you, and it may happen that ye love a thing which is bad for you. Allah knoweth, ye know not." Istikharah doesn't stop the person deciding. It changes who they're deciding with.

1085.title: Together, twenty-seven times
1085.hook: prayer in congregation is twenty-seven times better than alone (Bukhari)
1085.howItsDone: Muslims pray in congregation at mosques, in homes and at work, standing in straight rows behind an imam; even two people can pray together, with one leading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, istikharah: two units and a du'a that asks God to choose the good. Today the prayer stops being alone.

Sunset in a small apartment, two roommates home from work, a pot on the stove. The sunset prayer has come in. Each could pray alone, in separate rooms, and be back at dinner in minutes. Instead one steps forward onto the rug, and the other stands at his right side. One voice says Allahu akbar, and two people bow at once. No mosque, no crowd, no microphone. A leader, a follower, and a room that smells of onions. Today's word is what those two just made.
screen: `SUNSET, TWO ROOMMATES.` → `ONE STEPS FORWARD.` → `ONE VOICE, TWO BOW.`

segments.voice: Jama'ah means congregation, the gathered group. First, the number in today's title. Ibn Umar reported, in Sahih al-Bukhari, that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said prayer in congregation is better than prayer alone by twenty-seven degrees. Right beside it, Bukhari records another companion's report that says twenty-five. Scholars offer ways to read the two together; the hadith doesn't explain the arithmetic. Both agree on direction: together is more. Second, the Qur'an. Pickthall's translation of surah two: "bow your heads with those who bow." With. Third, the rows. The Prophet told them to straighten their rows, and said straightening them is part of establishing the prayer. Anas, his servant, described them standing shoulder to shoulder and foot to foot. In a row, the person beside you is whoever arrived next, and the row doesn't check anyone's bank balance. Fourth, who is called. Scholars differ on how binding congregation is for men: the Hanbali school treats it as obligatory, others as a communal duty or a strongly stressed sunnah. And Bukhari records the Prophet saying: do not keep the women servants of God from the mosques of God. Now look back at the week. Stand now, at the iqamah. The sunnah around it. End the night odd. Awake for him. The forenoon prayer. Choose for me. All but the first can be done alone, in a dark bedroom or a quiet office. The week ends by stepping into the row.
screen: `TWENTY-SEVEN, OR TWENTY-FIVE.` · `BOW WITH THOSE WHO BOW.` · `SHOULDER TO SHOULDER.` · `THE WEEK STEPS INTO THE ROW.` · then, large: `TOGETHER IS MORE.`

segments.voice: See a row in your mind and who might stand in it with you, a neighbor, a parent, a stranger from the bus, and feel where your shoulder would touch theirs. If you pray, you can pray one prayer today in congregation, at a mosque or with even one other person at home. If you don't, you can share one thing you'd usually do alone: a meal, a walk, a job around the house.
Jama'ah. The congregation: prayer in rows, together, counted in the hadith as twenty-seven degrees above prayer alone. Today's word.
Your line: together is more. Tomorrow, the voice that speaks to the row on Friday.
